title: The Hidden Culture Clues Buyers Miss (And Why They Matter)

 The Hidden Culture Clues Buyers Miss (And Why They Matter)
Hi Sara,
You can’t put company culture on a spreadsheet. But that doesn’t mean you should ignore it.
This week, I had the good fortune of catching up with some past clients—people who’ve bought accounting practices and made it through their first tax season. 
And when I asked, “What do you wish you’d known before closing?” the biggest theme wasn’t about financials, legal hurdles, or even client retention.
It was employee culture.
The Culture Trap Buyers Walk Into
When you buy a business, you’re often not allowed to meet employees until the deal is done. So how do you know if you’re walking into a functional, well-run team… or an office that runs on chaos and quiet quitting?
You can’t just ask, “Is this a toxic workplace?” (I mean, you could, but good luck getting an honest answer.) Instead, you have to get creative.
What Can You Look For?
➝ How does the seller talk about their team?
One of the best signals I’ve seen? A seller who voluntarily adds details about their employees beyond just salary and hours worked. 
I once saw a seller include a column in their diligence spreadsheet that listed each employee’s strengths—totally unprompted. That’s a seller who values their team, and that’s a great sign for culture.
➝ How does the seller behave in negotiations?
If they’re defensive, aggressive, or flat-out dishonest during the deal process, guess what? 
That’s likely how they’ve run the company, too. Employees don’t thrive in that kind of environment.
➝ What’s turnover like?
 Longevity can be a sign of stability—but it can also mean people feel stuck and unmotivated. 
Ask about how employees feel about leadership and why people have left in the past.
If Culture Isn’t What You Expected…
Not every transition is smooth. Some buyers step into a workplace that isn’t what they’d hoped for. The good news? Culture can be fixed.
There are incredible CPA-specific coaches who help firms navigate post-close team issues. (Brian Amann and Douglas Slaybaugh come to mind—fantastic resources.) 
But it takes patience and intentionality to rebuild trust and create the culture you want.
So, if you’re in diligence right now, take an extra beat to ask the right questions. It could save you a lot of headaches after closing.
And if you’ve been through this already, I’d love to hear from you—what do you wish you had known before closing?
To smarter deals,
Sara Sharp
Partner, SK&S Law Group
Business Consultant & Founder of Deal Academy
